summary: Sirach 44 begins the book's praise of Israel's ancestors by naming the kinds of honor, wisdom, leadership, prophecy, artistry, wealth, and peace associated with earlier generations. It reflects on remembered and forgotten lives, then praises mercy and righteousness through enduring offspring, covenant, and communal remembrance. The chapter starts the named sequence with Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, emphasizing covenant, blessing, testing, inheritance, and the twelve tribes.
whyItMatters: This chapter opens the book's final historical praise section, where wisdom is shown through remembered ancestors rather than only through maxims. It turns instruction into collective memory, while still acknowledging that not everyone from the past is remembered.

context.author: Yeshua, or Jesus, son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and Greek-reading Jews who received the grandson's translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, Torah, and ancestral writings central to Jewish public and educational life.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction and poetic praise of ancestors, using compact lines, catalogues, and remembered examples.

outline.heading: A Call to Praise the Ancestors
outline.note: The chapter opens by urging praise for the ancestors and attributing their glory to the Lord's mighty work.

outline.heading: Kinds of Honor in Earlier Generations
outline.note: The praised figures include rulers, counselors, prophets, teachers, composers, writers, wealthy people of ability, and people who lived peaceably.

outline.heading: Remembered and Forgotten Names
outline.note: Some ancestors left a name for later praise, while others vanished from public memory; the passage then honors enduring mercy and righteous deeds.

outline.heading: Enduring Offspring and Praise
outline.note: The legacy of the righteous is described through offspring, covenant, lasting glory, peaceful burial, living names, declared wisdom, and congregational praise.

outline.heading: Enoch and Noah
outline.note: Enoch is remembered as pleasing the Lord and being taken up; Noah is remembered as righteous, preserving the race through wrath and receiving covenants after the flood.

outline.heading: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
outline.note: Abraham is praised for covenant faithfulness and blessing; the same assurance is continued through Isaac and made to rest on Jacob, whose portions are distributed among twelve tribes.

keyVerses.text: Let us now praise famous men, our ancestors in their generations.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter's purpose: praise for remembered ancestors across generations.

keyVerses.text: But these were men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten.
keyVerses.why: This verse makes mercy and righteous deeds central to the ancestors' lasting legacy, alongside the chapter's concern with names, descendants, and public memory.

keyVerses.text: People will declare their wisdom. The congregation proclaims their praise.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows that the chapter is not only listing names; it portrays public memory as an act of praise.

keyVerses.text: who kept the law of the Most High, and was taken into covenant with him. In his flesh he established the covenant. When he was tested, he was found faithful.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the praise of Abraham in law, covenant, testing, and faithfulness.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by praising ancestors?
questions.answer: The chapter begins a new movement in Sirach, shifting from general wisdom teaching into praise of Israel's ancestors. The opening call frames memory as instruction: earlier generations are remembered for glory, wisdom, leadership, mercy, righteousness, and covenant faithfulness.

questions.question: Who are the “famous men” in this chapter?
questions.answer: At first the chapter speaks broadly about honored people from earlier generations: rulers, counselors, prophets, leaders, teachers, musicians, writers, and wealthy people of ability. Only later does it name particular figures: Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

questions.question: Does the chapter say every person from the past is remembered?
questions.answer: No. Some ancestors left a celebrated name, while others disappeared from public memory. The following lines praise mercy, righteous deeds, and a legacy carried through descendants and covenant. Being forgotten is not itself presented as proof that someone lacked virtue.

questions.question: What does “their children are within the covenant” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the phrase links the praised ancestors with continuing descendants and covenant belonging. The surrounding verses speak of offspring, children, remaining forever, and glory not being blotted out, so the emphasis is on an enduring family and covenant legacy.

questions.question: Why does the chapter mention burial if the names still live?
questions.answer: Verse 14 holds two ideas together: the ancestors died and were buried, yet their name continues through later generations. The chapter is not denying death; it is describing a form of honor that outlasts death through memory, wisdom, offspring, and praise.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about Enoch?
questions.answer: The chapter says only that Enoch pleased the Lord, was taken up, and became an example of repentance to all generations. Readers may connect this with other traditions about Enoch, but this chapter itself keeps the statement brief and uses him as the first named example in the praise sequence.

questions.question: What role does Noah play in this chapter?
questions.answer: Noah is praised as perfect and righteous, and as the one through whom the race was kept alive during wrath and flood. The chapter also says everlasting covenants were made with him so that all flesh would not again be blotted out by a flood.

questions.question: Why is Abraham central near the end of the chapter?
questions.answer: Abraham receives the fullest treatment in this chapter. He is called a great father of many nations, linked with law and covenant, tested and found faithful, and given an oath concerning blessing, multiplied offspring, and land from sea to sea.

questions.question: How do Isaac and Jacob continue Abraham's story here?
questions.answer: The chapter says the same assurance was established in Isaac for Abraham's sake. It then says the blessing rested on Jacob, who received inheritance and whose portions were distributed among twelve tribes.

glossary.def: Earlier generations whom the chapter calls readers to praise and remember.
Successive ages or family lines; the chapter uses the word for both the ancestors' own time and the continuing memory of their names.
A binding relationship or assurance connected here with Abraham, Isaac, Noah, and the descendants who remain within it.
Descendants; the chapter repeatedly uses this word to describe the continuing legacy of the praised ancestors.
The gathered people who proclaim the praise of the remembered wise and righteous.
